questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a tariff?
options: A tax on imported goods, which raises their price in the domestic market
A physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
A payment by government to domestic producers
A ban on trade with a particular country
questions.why: A tariff raises the price paid in the domestic market from the world price to the world price plus the tariff.
whyNot: That is an import quota.
That is a domestic subsidy.
That is an embargo.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines an import quota?
options: A physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported in a period
A tax on goods entering the country
A minimum price at which imports may be sold
A requirement that imports meet local safety standards
questions.why: A quota caps the quantity regardless of price, so no amount of cost cutting gets more product through.
whyNot: That is a tariff.
That is a price floor, not a quota.
That is a non-tariff barrier.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a domestic subsidy?
options: A payment by government to domestic producers, lowering their costs relative to imports
A tax on imported goods
A payment by consumers to domestic producers
A limit on the quantity a domestic firm may produce
questions.why: Subsidies are paid by the taxpayer rather than the consumer, which makes them politically easier and no less distorting.
whyNot: That is a tariff.
Consumers pay prices, not subsidies.
That is a production quota.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a non-tariff barrier?
options: Any restriction on imports other than a tax, such as standards, licensing or labelling rules
A tariff set at a very low rate
A voluntary agreement between two businesses
A tax on exports
questions.why: Non-tariff barriers are the fastest-growing form of protection because they are hard to challenge when dressed as consumer protection.
whyNot: A low tariff is still a tariff.
A private agreement is not a government barrier.
That is an export tax, which is not a barrier to imports.

questions.stem: A component costs $40 and a 15% tariff is imposed. What is the tariff per unit?
whyNot: That treats the percentage as a dollar amount.
That misplaces the decimal point.
That is the new cost per unit, not the tariff.

questions.stem: A tariff adds $6.00 per unit and the business uses 50,000 units a year. What is the extra annual cost?
whyNot: That adds rather than multiplies.
That divides rather than multiplies.
That misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten.

questions.stem: A tariff cuts contribution per unit from $22 to $16. Fixed costs are $250,000. What happens to break-even output?
options: It rises from about 11,364 to about 15,625 units
It falls from about 15,625 to about 11,364 units
It stays the same, because fixed costs are unchanged
It rises from about 11,364 to about 12,500 units
whyNot: A lower contribution raises break-even, not lowers it.
Break-even depends on contribution as well as fixed costs.
That uses an incorrect contribution figure.

questions.stem: Who bears the cost of a tariff on an imported input?
options: The business using the input, and ultimately its customers
Only the foreign producer
Only the government
Nobody, because tariffs raise revenue
questions.why: A tariff on steel protects steelmakers and raises costs for every manufacturer that buys steel, which is the effect students most often miss.
whyNot: The foreign producer may cut its price, but the importer pays the duty.
Government receives the revenue rather than bearing the cost.
The revenue is paid by someone, which is the point.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the infant industry argument for protection?
options: A new domestic industry needs temporary protection until it is large enough to compete
Protection should be given to the oldest industries in an economy
Industries serving children should be protected
Protection should apply only to agriculture
questions.why: The standard objection is that temporary protection rarely ends, because the industry has every incentive to lobby to keep it.
whyNot: Age of the industry is not the argument.
The term refers to the industry being new, not its customers.
The argument is not sector-specific.

questions.stem: Why is a quota worse than a tariff for an exporting business?
options: No amount of cost cutting gets more product through a fixed quantity limit
Quotas raise the exporter's own tax bill
Quotas are always set at zero
Quotas apply only to services
questions.why: A tariff gives a certain cost and an uncertain volume; a quota gives a certain limit on volume whatever the exporter does.
whyNot: The exporter's domestic tax position is unaffected.
A zero quota would be an embargo, which is a different instrument.
Quotas typically apply to goods.

questions.stem: Why does a quota raise the domestic price without generating government revenue?
options: The gain goes to whoever holds the import licences rather than to the government
The government refuses to collect it
Prices do not rise under a quota
The revenue goes to the foreign government
questions.why: This is a real difference from a tariff, where the government collects the duty.
whyNot: There is no duty to collect under a quantity limit.
Restricting quantity raises the price.
No revenue passes to any government.

questions.stem: Why can retaliation turn a gain from protection into a loss?
options: A tariff imposed to protect one industry invites a tariff on another country's exports, harming businesses that were never protected
Retaliation always removes the original tariff
Retaliation only affects government revenue
Retaliation is prohibited under all circumstances
questions.why: The businesses harmed by retaliation are usually not the ones that were protected, which is the key evaluative point.
whyNot: Retaliation adds barriers rather than removing them.
Exporters lose sales, which is a direct business effect.
The WTO permits retaliation where a member breaks the rules.

questions.stem: Why may protection leave a domestic industry less competitive in the long run?
options: Protection removes the pressure to become efficient, so the industry becomes more dependent on it continuing
Protection raises the industry's costs directly
Protection forces the industry to export
Protection reduces domestic demand for the product
questions.why: Short-run relief is real; the long-run danger is a permanently uncompetitive industry lobbying to keep the protection.
whyNot: Protection raises the price it receives, not its costs.
Protection is aimed at the domestic market.
Protection raises the quantity domestically supplied.

questions.stem: What happens to domestic production when a tariff is imposed?
options: It rises, because the higher price makes more output profitable
It falls, because prices are higher
It stays the same, because supply is fixed
It rises only if the tariff revenue is given to producers
questions.why: Domestic supply rises, domestic consumption falls, and imports are squeezed from both ends.
whyNot: Producers receive the higher price, so they supply more.
Domestic supply responds to price.
The supply response comes from the price, not from any transfer.

questions.stem: Why can a non-tariff barrier cost a business more than a tariff would?
options: Redesigning a product to meet one market's standards can cost more than the duty
Non-tariff barriers are always set at higher rates
Non-tariff barriers are collected twice
Non-tariff barriers apply to domestic producers only
questions.why: Compliance and delay are the real costs, and they are harder to challenge as protectionist than a tariff is.
whyNot: They are not expressed as rates at all.
There is no duty to collect.
They apply to imports, which is what makes them a barrier.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines dumping?
options: Selling exports below cost, or below the home price, to capture a foreign market
Exporting surplus goods at the full market price
Disposing of waste in another country
Selling goods at a discount in the domestic market
questions.why: An anti-dumping duty is a defensible response, though proving dumping is difficult and the accusation is easily misused.
whyNot: Selling at the market price is ordinary exporting.
That is waste export, a different issue.
Domestic discounting is not dumping.

questions.stem: Why is a tariff generally ineffective at correcting a trade deficit?
options: Imports are also inputs, and retaliation reduces exports
Tariffs cannot be applied to all goods
Trade deficits are always caused by exchange rates alone
Tariffs increase the volume of imports
questions.why: Raising input costs damages domestic producers, and lost exports offset any reduction in imports.
whyNot: Tariffs can be applied broadly; effectiveness is the issue.
Deficits have several causes.
Tariffs reduce imports; the problem is the side effects.
